area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the power-off stall at commercial-pilot depth, fly it from the right seat while you explain it, and teach it to a learner: brief it, demonstrate it, supervise practice, and spot and fix the common errors.
why: Most stall accidents start with an unplanned stall at low altitude, with no room to finish the recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The power-off stall rehearses the approach and landing version of that accident, such as a crossed-control base to final turn or raising the nose alone to fix a high sink rate on final [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]]. As a flight instructor you must be able to give stall training [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]], and your learners will copy the way you demonstrate it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

prereading.what: Impending and full stalls, recognition, AOA indicators, stall characteristics, the recovery template and the power-off stall procedure.
prereading.label: AFH 5-12 to 5-17

prereading.what: Turning power-off stalls, secondary, accelerated, cross-control and elevator trim stalls, the 18 common errors and spin awareness.
prereading.label: AFH 5-18 to 5-22

prereading.what: What moves the stall speed, distractions, contamination, stall recognition, the types of stalls and recovery.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C 100 to 106

prereading.what: The flight training plan for stalls that a CFI is expected to give, including power-off stalls with distractions.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C 200

prereading.what: Demonstration-performance, telling-and-doing, positive exchange of flight controls and the use of distractions.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-10

prereading.what: Managing risk while you instruct: safe altitude, guarding the controls, ceilings and stalls below clouds.
prereading.label: AIH 10-3 to 10-8

prereading.what: Stall aerodynamics: CL-MAX, root-first stall design, why the nose drops and the critical AOA.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-25 to 5-27

warmup: Think first: your learner has done three good power-off stalls with you on the controls beside them. On the fourth, at the stall break, they pull the yoke hard back into their lap and stiffen up. The left wing is dropping. What do you say, what do you do with your hands, and in what order? Then ask yourself: what could you have done in the briefing that would have made this less likely?

key_terms.def: The AOA at which the wing stalls. A given airplane always stalls at the same AOA, whatever its airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
The AOA has set off a stall warning but has not yet reached the critical AOA [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
The critical AOA is exceeded; typically an uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot readily be stopped, perhaps with an uncommanded roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
Also called an approach-to-landing stall: practiced in normal approach conditions and configuration [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]].
A wing twist that gives the tips a slightly lower AOA than the roots, so the roots stall first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
Knowing the gap between the AOA you are flying and the critical AOA. An AOA indicator shows it directly [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Lift divided by weight, in G. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].
A stall that follows a stall recovery, from rushing the recovery before flying speed returns [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].
A four-phase way to teach a skill: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
The flight version of demonstration-performance: instructor tells and does, learner tells and instructor does, learner tells and does, then learner does and instructor evaluates [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
A three-step spoken handover, 'You have the flight controls', 'I have the flight controls', 'You have the flight controls', so there is never doubt about who is flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
A learner self-assessment followed by the instructor's assessment and a discussion comparing the two [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

body.p: A stall happens when the AOA, the angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind, goes past the critical AOA. It can happen at any airspeed, in any attitude and at any power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Practicing stalls on purpose teaches the conditions that lead to one, how to recognize it coming, and the right response [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

The power-off stall is the approach-to-landing stall. It is practiced in normal approach conditions and configuration [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]] [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Each version matches a real accident setup you will describe to your learner:

bullets: Straight ahead: the stall you could get stretching a glide after an engine failure, or when low on the approach [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Shallow turn: the stall you could get by misusing the controls in the turn from base to final [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
All flap settings: so the learner knows how the airplane handles after a mechanical failure, icing or another abnormal situation [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

body.p: Stalls are practiced to two levels. Impending: recover at the first stall warning. Full: hold the attitude until the critical AOA is exceeded [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The AFH says training should teach the same recovery for both [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. On the CFI checkride the evaluator chooses which one, and you and the evaluator must review this Area of Operation in the preflight briefing (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X note; AI.X.C.S8).

callout.text: The CFI ACS says the evaluation of a power-off stall recovery should not demand a set altitude loss or that you hold altitude during the recovery, because many things affect it (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task C note). Some altitude loss is expected [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

Application: tie every stall you teach to its real-world twin. Before the first power-off stall, ask the learner where in the pattern this could bite them. A learner who can name the setup is more likely to spot it later.

check.q: Which real flight situation does the turning power-off stall simulate?
check.a: A stall from misusing the controls in the turn from base leg to final approach [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

chunks.title: Aerodynamics: AOA and what moves the stall speed

body.p: Start the ground lesson with AOA, not airspeed. The stall is the result of too much AOA, not too little airspeed [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]]. The lift coefficient climbs with AOA to a peak, CL-MAX, then falls off. The wing still makes some lift; it just cannot hold level flight [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. The critical AOA is roughly 16 to 20 degrees depending on the design, and each airplane has only one [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

The published 1 G stall speed is valid only in unaccelerated flight, coordinated, at one weight (usually maximum gross) and one CG (usually the forward limit) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Teach K2 as a list of things that change the speed at which the fixed critical AOA is reached:

head: Factor
What it does
Source
rows: Angle of attack
The only thing that stalls the wing; exceed the critical AOA and the wing stalls
Airspeed
Slower flight needs more AOA for the same lift, until the critical AOA is passed
Load factor
Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor: 45 knots at 1 G becomes 90 knots at 4 G
Power setting
Power adds lift without more AOA, and propwash over the wing gives an immediate boost, so power-on stall speeds are lower
Weight
More weight needs more AOA for the extra lift, so the stall speed rises
Center of gravity
Forward CG reaches the stalling AOA at a higher airspeed; aft CG needs less elevator to stall and makes recovery harder
Airplane attitude
Not a reliable cue: the airplane can be stalled in any attitude
Yaw effects
Engine torque yaws the nose as power comes in, needing right rudder; yaw at the stall is what starts a spin

body.p: Configuration matters too. Flaps generally raise the lifting ability of the wing and lower the stall speed, which is why the bottom of the white arc (landing configuration) sits below the bottom of the green arc (clean) [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100c]]. In the PHAK sample table, gear and flaps down with power off stalls at 57 knots wings level and 68 knots at 45 degrees of bank [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

Why the nose drops: the center of lift sits behind the CG and the tail's down force balances it. At the stall both fade, so the airplane pitches down about its CG, the AOA drops and the wing flies again [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. With the CG behind the aft limit the elevator may not be able to lower the nose, and the airplane can stay stalled to the ground [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

callout.text: Application: a hand and a pencil make a good ground demo. Hold the pencil as the relative wind and tilt your flat hand past it. The learner sees that AOA, not nose attitude, is what changed.

check.q: Why can a learner stall at a higher indicated airspeed than the POH figure on a hot day with a heavy, forward-loaded airplane in a 20-degree turn?
check.a: The POH figure assumes 1 G, coordinated, and a set weight and CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Bank adds load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] and weight raises the stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]]. Altitude and temperature have little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

chunks.title: Stall characteristics and recognition by sight, sound and feel

body.p: Different designs stall differently; geometry, CG, wing design and high-lift devices all play a part, so know the stall behavior of the airplane you teach in [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

bullets: Root-first design: most trainers stall at the root first, and washout keeps the tips at a lower AOA so the ailerons keep some effect [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Stall strips on the leading edge are another way to make the root stall first [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
Rectangular wing: tends to stall at the root first with adequate stall warning and aileron effect [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].
Elliptical wing: little advance warning of a complete stall, and lateral control may be difficult [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

Power-off versus power-on: in a power-off stall the buffet and shaking are less noticeable. In a power-off 1 G stall the main cue may be the elevator full aft against the stop and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

body.p: Recognition is learned by sight, sound and feel [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Teach each cue by name, and have the learner call it out loud the moment it appears (AI.X.C.S7):

head: Cue
What the learner notices
Source
rows: Sight
Not foolproof, since a stall can happen in any attitude, but pitch awareness still matters
Sound
The noise of the air along the airplane changes as speed drops
Feel
Control pressures get lighter, bigger movements are needed and the response is slower; a mushy feel
Kinesthesia
The seat-of-the-pants sense of changes in speed and direction, useful to a trained pilot in visual flight
Buffet
Buffeting, uncontrollable pitching or vibration just before the stall
Full stall
An uncommanded nose drop that cannot readily be stopped, perhaps with an uncommanded roll

body.p: An AOA indicator, if installed, shows the margin to the critical AOA directly [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Some account for flap position and some do not [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. The AFH asks ground and flight instructors to get training from someone who knows AOA indicators before teaching with one [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

callout.text: The AIH notes that stall recovery cannot really be learned until the learner has some experience in normal flight, and that time and practice are needed to build a perception of the stall [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. Expect recognition to grow over several lessons, not one.

check.q: In a power-off 1 G stall, which cue may be the strongest, and why does that matter for your teaching?
check.a: The elevator full aft against the stop with a high descent rate, since the buffet is weaker than in a power-on stall [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Point it out, or the learner may wait for a buffet that hardly comes.

chunks.title: Stall warning indicators: range, limits and normal operations

body.p: Range and limitations of stall warning indicators (R2). Teach what the warning can and cannot do:

bullets: The rule: the airplane must give a clear and distinctive stall warning with enough margin to prevent an inadvertent stall [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]].

Buffet versus device: the warning can be built-in aerodynamic buffet rather than a device. Most vintage airplanes and many light-sport and experimental airplanes have no stall warning device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Stall horn range: many devices warn 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. That is typical, not a promise for your airplane.

Contamination: in some icing conditions the stall can come with little or none of the usual cues, such as buffet, horn or shaker [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]], at a lower AOA and a higher airspeed than normal [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102b]].
Autopilot: an autopilot can mask some of the cues the pilot would feel [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102c]].
AOA indicators: limited by calibration, unheated probes or vanes, indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

body.p: Stall warnings during normal operations (R3). At the landing attitude the airplane is approaching a stall [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]; application: so a brief warning right in the flare is expected. A warning anywhere else is a call to act. In the AFH's hot, high departure example the airplane stops climbing as the pilot keeps raising the nose, and then the horn sounds [[24:101|AFH 4-15]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]]. When a warning comes, the AC says the response should be instinctive: add power, lower the nose and/or shallow the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

callout.text: Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues after recovery is a listed common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Train every cue, so a failed horn does not mean a missed stall.
Application: before the first stall, have the learner find the stall warning vane or opening on the preflight and say what kind of warning this airplane has. It makes R2 concrete.

check.q: A learner says, 'The horn always gives me plenty of warning.' What two limits do you point out?
check.a: Many airplanes have no warning device, only buffet [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], and with ice the stall can come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]].

chunks.title: How real power-off stalls happen, and the environment

body.p: Factors and situations that lead to a power-off stall (K4, R1). Many stall/spin accidents have come from crossed-control turns from base to final, from trying to fix a high sink rate on final with pitch alone, and from poor airspeed control in the pattern [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]]. Loss of control is the number one root cause of fatal accidents, and half of the maneuvering-phase fatal accidents involve stall or spin [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

head: Situation
Why it ends in a stall
Prevention to teach
rows: Low final approach
Raising the nose without power slows the airplane toward the critical AOA [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Add power as you raise the nose, do not retract flaps, go around if in doubt [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Slow final approach
The wing works near the critical AOA and may stall or sink hard [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Add power early; if too slow and too low, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Overshooting base to final
Steep bank, inside rudder and back pressure: a skidding cross-control stall that may become a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Go around; be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees this low and never skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
High round out
Holding the round out raises the AOA to critical and the airplane drops in [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Hold the attitude, add a little power, go around if the nose must come down a lot [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Distraction in the pattern
Airspeed slips while the pilot does another task [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]
Application: fly first; brief tasks before entering the pattern

body.p: A spin needs a stall plus yaw. Mishandled yaw at the stall makes a spin more likely, so keeping the nose from yawing is the key to averting one [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
Environmental elements (R6):

bullets: Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA, and the stall often comes while the pilot fights to hold the path on a gusty approach. Carry a higher approach speed in moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

Microbursts: a pilot who reduced power and lowered the nose for the headwind shear is nose-low and power-low when the tailwind shear hits, which can cause a stall or a landing short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

High density altitude: indicated stall speed hardly changes, so fly the normal indicated approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. But the engine makes less power [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]]. Application: expect a weaker go-around and more altitude loss in a recovery.

callout.text: Application: teach prevention as energy management on the approach: stabilized speed, pitch and power used together, and an early go-around. Then the power-off stall becomes what happens when that plan fails.

check.q: Your learner is low on final and raises the nose to stretch it. Which K4 trap is this, and what is the fix?
check.a: Raising pitch without power slows the airplane toward the critical AOA; add power as the nose comes up, and go around if in doubt [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

body.p: The most important action in any impending or full stall is to reduce the AOA. Pilots who put power and holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The AFH gives a generic template adapted from one written by major airplane makers; the manufacturer's current procedure comes first when published [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

bullets: 1. Disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot, if equipped [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
2. Pitch nose-down until the impending stall indications are gone; nose-down trim only if needed, since too much trim can make things worse [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
3. Roll the wings level, cancelling yaw with rudder so the stall does not become a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
4. Add power as needed, smoothly, with rudder and elevator to stop yaw and pitch-up. Power cuts altitude loss but does not end a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
5. Retract speedbrakes or spoilers, if equipped [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
6. Return to the desired flightpath with smooth, coordinated inputs, avoiding a secondary stall and watching terrain [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: In a single-engine trainer without an autopilot or spoilers only four steps apply: reduce AOA until the stall warning stops, roll wings level, add power as needed while coordinated, return to the flightpath [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Recovery is complete when the airplane is back on the desired flightpath with enough airspeed, good control effectiveness and no stall warning [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

How much push: every airplane needs a different amount, and too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by putting a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. After a simulated approach stall, establish a positive rate of climb as in a go-around, then retract flaps and gear as necessary [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]; the ACS wants the manufacturer's configuration and acceleration to VX or VY (AI.X.C.S9). Take the flaps up in small steps so the airplane can accelerate [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: Never let the airspeed or tachometer reach their high-speed red lines during a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].
Unload, level, power, fly: AOA first, wings second, throttle third, flightpath last.

check.q: Why does the AFH say not to try to control the bank before reducing the AOA?
check.a: Roll stability and roll control improve a lot once the wings are flying again, and aileron on a stalled wing can deepen the stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

body.p: These three stalls are what a power-off stall turns into when the learner's hands get ahead of the airplane. You will demonstrate them as a CFI, so know each by name.

bullets: Secondary stall: the critical AOA is exceeded again after a recovery, because the nose was not lowered enough, the recovery was rushed, or power alone was used [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. The urge to pull up grows near the ground [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Fix: do the recovery again [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

Accelerated stall: any stall above 1 G, so at a higher airspeed. Common in badly flown turns, stall and spin recoveries, dive pull-outs and overshot base to final turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. They tend to be more aggressive and can surprise a pilot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Pulling too fast on a power-off stall entry is a listed error for exactly this reason [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Cross-control stall: aileron one way, rudder the other at the critical AOA. Little warning, a sudden bank change and possibly a roll toward inverted, the usual start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: The turning power-off stall shows the link. Keep it coordinated with a constant bank. In a slip, the outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly; in a skid, the bank may steepen to a dangerous attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Do not try to stall on a set heading, but expect the stall within about 90 degrees of turn, like a base to final turn [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

AC 61-67C gives you two teaching demonstrations built on the power-off stall: show how errors in flap retraction can cause a secondary stall, and recover then climb with flaps extended at a higher than normal pitch (a secondary stall follows), or retract the flaps rapidly while holding that pitch (a secondary stall or settling with altitude loss may follow) [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]] [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

callout.text: Secondary and cross-control stalls are demonstration-only maneuvers for pilot certification; only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform them on a practical test [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: During a turning power-off stall your learner is holding left aileron and right rudder at the break. What stall is developing and what is the risk?
check.a: A cross-control stall, which can come with little warning and roll toward inverted, usually the start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Collision hazards (R7). A stall descends, so clear at and below your altitude and make sure enough altitude is available [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. In a high-wing airplane raise the wing toward the turn and look; in a low-wing airplane lower it and look. Have the learner call 'clear' left, right, above and below out loud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Many programs use two 90-degree turns in opposite directions, and the instructor should insist on a clearing procedure before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. The AIH reminds you to make lookout a shared job: both of you are responsible for see and avoid [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

Altitude (S2). Plan to finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, or higher if the POH recommends it [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] (AI.X.C.S2). Use the highest terrain in the area and your airplane's own altitude loss. Never teach stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness and disorientation (R8):

bullets: Distractions: most stall/spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted from flying. Intentional stall practice seldom caused an accident; the danger was inadvertent stalls from distraction in routine flight [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Task prioritization: once airborne, budgeting time and prioritizing tasks can leave enough time to do them without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Teach 'fly first' during every setup.

Loss of situational awareness: knowing position, flightpath, other traffic and the environment [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Losing it and failing to return to the desired flightpath or follow ATC is a listed stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Disorientation: spatial disorientation is a lack of orientation about the position, attitude or movement of the airplane [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. The seat-of-the-pants sense is useful mainly to a trained pilot in visual flight [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], so recover by the outside horizon cross-checked with the instruments.

callout.text: ADS-B In helps, but in some airspace not all aircraft show on it. Limit the time you spend looking at instruments or tablets, and scan the whole sky [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

check.q: The ceiling over the practice area is lower than the altitude you need for stalls. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Do not teach stalls below the cloud layer [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; options include changing the lesson, using a simulation device or ground school, or rescheduling [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Fly it while you explain it

body.p: On the CFI checkride you demonstrate and explain at the same time. Use the AFH procedure, adjusted by your POH, and say each step as you fly it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

bullets: 1. Brief: impending or full, straight or turning, configuration, and the altitude, heading and airspeed to return to (AI.X.C.S8, S10).
2. Clear the area at and below you and confirm the entry altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] (AI.X.C.S1, S2). Say: 'Clear left, clear right, nothing below.'

3. Gear down if retractable, carburetor heat on if applicable, throttle back, and hold altitude until the speed slows to normal approach speed [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Say: 'Holding altitude while we slow to approach speed.'

4. Pitch smoothly to the normal approach attitude, extend flaps and adjust pitch to hold speed, then set idle [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] (AI.X.C.S3). Keep the ball centered throughout. Say: 'Approach configuration, idle, trimmed.'
5. Stabilize the descent at approach speed (AI.X.C.S4). Extra speed carried into the entry gives an abnormally nose-high attitude [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

6. Smoothly raise the nose to a stall attitude and hold it with elevator, wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] (AI.X.C.S5). In the turning version hold a constant bank, coordinated [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (AI.X.C.S6).
7. Call the first cue out loud (AI.X.C.S7). Impending: recover now. Full: keep holding the attitude until the full-stall cues appear [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
8. Recover: nose-down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinated, power as needed with right rudder [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] (AI.X.C.S8).
9. Positive rate of climb, then flaps and gear as the manufacturer recommends, accelerating to VX or VY [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] (AI.X.C.S9).
10. Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the evaluator gave (AI.X.C.S10).

head: Element
CFI ACS standard (AI.X.C)
rows: S2 Entry altitude
Task completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ASEL)
S3 Configuration
Approach or landing configuration, as specified by the evaluator; coordinated throughout
S6 Heading or bank
Specified heading, ±10° if straight; specified bank not to exceed 20°, ±5° if turning; until an impending or full stall occurs
S7 Recognition
Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall
S8 Recovery
At the first indication or after a full stall, as specified by the evaluator
S9 Climb
Configure as the manufacturer recommends; accelerate to VX or VY
S10 Return
Altitude, heading and airspeed specified by the evaluator

callout.text: If the demonstration does not match your explanation, say so right away and explain why [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. An unexplained wobble teaches the learner that wobbles are fine.

check.q: During your right-seat demonstration of a turning power-off stall, how much can the bank vary from the specified value?
check.a: Plus or minus 5 degrees, with the specified bank not more than 20 degrees, until the impending or full stall occurs (AI.X.C.S6).

body.p: Pair the flight with ground instruction. The AIH says progress on stalls through flight instruction alone is slower than when the types and aerodynamics are discussed on the ground first, and you should review the task before flight even if it was covered in ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].
Use the telling-and-doing technique, the flight version of demonstration-performance [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]:

head: Step
What it looks like for the power-off stall
Source
rows: Preparation (explanation)
Ground brief: purpose, the real-world twin, the setup, the cues, the recovery and the standards. Cover safety and invite questions
Instructor tells, instructor does
You fly one, describing attitudes and power settings as you go, in the same order you briefed it
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner talks you through one while you fly. Misunderstandings show up before they are on the controls
Learner tells, learner does
The learner flies and says each step aloud; you watch for errors and guard the controls
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Debrief with a self-assessment first, then yours, then compare (collaborative assessment)

body.p: Building blocks: start with impending stalls, straight ahead, then add the full stall, the turning version and other flap settings. When teaching more than one skill, the simple-to-complex strategy keeps the learner from getting frustrated [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

Add realism. AC 61-67C's training plan for power-off stalls: have the learner do a full-flap, gear-extended, power-off stall with the correct recovery and cleanup, and note the altitude lost. Then repeat it while you distract them during the stall and recovery, and talk about the effect [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]]. The FAA stall awareness study behind AC 61-67C found that simulating scenarios with distractions is the most effective training method [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]], and the AIH says the same [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

Correcting errors: safety permitting, let the learner go part way into a mistake and find the way out; a learner who never gets to correct an error learns the maneuver poorly [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. To check real understanding, have them vary the maneuver slightly or combine it with another [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Principle of primacy: get it right the first time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Your first demonstration sets the habit, so fly it exactly as you want it copied, including the clearing turns [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

check.q: In telling-and-doing, which step lets you catch a learner's misunderstanding before they are flying, and how?
check.a: Learner tells, instructor does: the learner explains each step while you fly, so you hear any misunderstanding first [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Teaching safely: the anxious learner and the controls

body.p: Stalls are one of the maneuvers that make learners anxious. When introducing stalls, first review the aerodynamics, then describe the sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. An anxious learner facing a stall may go into a fight-or-flight response; you can take the procedure apart, demonstrate each stage of an impending or full stall, and let them practice the stages until they are comfortable [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. A learner who feels unsafe focuses on fleeing, not on the skill [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

Brief the positive exchange of flight controls before every stall lesson [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Guard the controls and be ready to take over. If you must, take the controls and calmly say 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be very strong, and there is nothing to gain by fighting them for the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. With hazardous maneuvers, be especially ready to take control on a learner's first attempts [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

bullets: Spin risk: practicing full stalls can result in inadvertent spins [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Altitude and a guarded set of controls are your mitigation [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].
Your limits: never let a learner exceed your limits, and do not exceed your own ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
The airplane: know the make and model before you instruct in it, from the POH or by flying it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Your own stall safety: the ACS says the applicant and the instructor or evaluator must always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin (CFI ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: Application: a freeze usually shows up as a learner pulling back at the break. Brief the exact words you will use, and use them. If the learner does not respond, take the controls with the three-step exchange and recover yourself.

check.q: Your learner tenses up and holds full back pressure at the stall break. What does the AIH say about taking control?
check.a: Take the controls and calmly say 'I have the flight controls'; there is nothing to gain from fighting an anxious learner for them [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

body.p: The AFH lists 18 common errors in intentional stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. On the CFI checkride the evaluator may play a learner and make them; you must analyze and correct (AI.X.C.S11). The ones that matter most for power-off stalls:

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to adequately clear the area
Straight into the setup with no turns or callouts
Insist on clearing before every maneuver, with 'clear' called aloud [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]
Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on entry
A quick yank, seat pressure, a sharp break above the usual speed
Raise the nose smoothly to the stall attitude and hold it [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Failure to keep a constant bank in turning stalls
Bank drifts past the briefed value as the speed decays
Hold a constant bank, coordinated, until the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Poor rudder coordination through stall and recovery
Ball out of center; nose yaws left as power comes in
Right rudder as power is added [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]; yaw at the stall leads to spins [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]
Recovering before the critical AOA on a full stall
Recovery at the first chirp when a full stall was asked for
Hold the attitude until the full-stall cues appear [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Failure to act in time on an impending stall
The learner lets it go into a full stall
Recover at the first indication; a full stall makes the impending stall unsatisfactory [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]
Leveling wings or adding power before reducing AOA
Aileron or throttle moves first, nose still high
Nose-down first until the warning stops, then wings, then power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Not holding nose-down input until the warning stops
Back pressure returns while the horn still sounds
Hold the forward input until the stall warning is eliminated [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Excessive forward pressure
Low or negative G, objects float, learner lifts from the seat
Use only enough to reduce AOA [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Secondary stall during recovery
Second buffet or break as the nose comes up
Let flying speed return before raising the nose [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]
Excessive airspeed buildup
Long dive after the recovery
Gradual pull-up as soon as the speed is safely above stall [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Losing situational awareness
Wrong heading or altitude after the climb, ATC instruction missed
Application: brief the return targets before the stall, so the learner knows where to fly after the recovery

body.p: Decide whether an error is a misunderstanding or a lack of motor skill. Having the learner think aloud makes that easy to tell [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. A misunderstanding goes back to the ground brief; a skill gap needs more practice.

callout.text: When you point out an error, give a concrete fix and try not to end the evaluation on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

check.q: Your learner recovers from a power-off stall, then raises the nose quickly and gets a second buffet. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: A secondary stall from rushing the recovery; lower the nose again and let flying speed return before raising it [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-7. Comparison of the teaching process, the demonstration-performance method and the telling-and-doing technique. (AIH 9-7)
f1.alt: A three-column table. Traditional teaching process: preparation, presentation, application, review and evaluation. Demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance supervision, evaluation. Telling-and-doing technique: preparation; instructor tells, instructor does; an orange marker for learner tells, instructor does; learner tells, learner does; learner does, instructor evaluates.

f2.caption: Figure 9-8. Positive exchange of flight controls. (AIH 9-9)
f2.alt: Three stacked green panels under the heading Positive Exchange of Flight Controls: 1, the instructor says 'You have the flight controls'; 2, the learner says 'I have the flight controls'; 3, the instructor again says 'You have the flight controls'.

f3.caption: Figure 5-11. Power-off stall and recovery. (AFH 5-17)
f3.alt: A high-wing airplane flies along a curved path: establish normal approach, raise nose and maintain heading, then when the stall occurs reduce angle of attack, roll wings level and add power as needed, then as flying speed returns stop the descent and establish a climb, maintain climb airspeed while raising gear, flaps and trim, and return to the desired flightpath.

f4.caption: Figure 5-10. Stall recovery template. (AFH 5-15)
f4.alt: A two-column table titled Stall Recovery Template listing the six recovery items and actions: disconnect wing leveler or autopilot; pitch nose-down until impending stall indications are eliminated, trim nose-down as needed; roll wings level; add thrust or power as needed; retract speed brakes or spoilers; return to the desired flight path.

f5.caption: Figure 5-13. Secondary stall. (AFH 5-19)
f5.alt: A high-wing airplane follows a curving path: an initial stall at the top left, a nose-down dive labeled incomplete or improper recovery, a pull-up into a second stall labeled secondary stall, and a second steep nose-down dive toward hills.

f6.caption: Figure 5-9. A conceptual representation of an AOA indicator. (AFH 5-14)
f6.alt: Three airfoil panels at 10, 16 and 17 degrees angle of attack, labeled A, B and C, with growing airflow separation. Next to them, three matching AOA indicator faces: A shows a blue ring, B shows two red chevrons at the top, C shows one red triangle at the top. Below, a graph of lift coefficient against angle of attack rises to about 2.0 near 15 degrees at B, then drops at C.

f7.caption: Figure 11-34. Stall speed table. (PHAK 11-28)
f7.alt: Stall speed table for a 2,750 lb airplane at level, 30, 45 and 60 degrees of bank. Gear and flaps up, power on: 54, 58, 64, 76 knots; power off: 65, 70, 77, 92 knots. Gear and flaps down, power on: 47, 50, 56, 66 knots; power off: 57, 62, 68, 81 knots. Matching mph values are also shown.

scenario.title: First power-off stalls with a nervous learner on a hazy day
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Your private pilot learner, who has flown 14 hours, is scheduled for a first power-off stall lesson in a high-wing trainer with a stall horn. It is a hazy summer afternoon with a scattered cloud layer about 3,500 ft AGL over the practice area, a field elevation of 1,200 ft and light chop. The learner tells you on the ramp that they did not sleep well because they are worried about stalls.

questions.q: Before you fly, how do you deal with the learner's worry about stalls?
questions.a: Treat the fear as normal, review the aerodynamics, describe the sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Consider breaking the stall into stages you demonstrate one at a time [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. Brief the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: Does the cloud layer limit the lesson?
questions.a: Yes. Stalls should be practiced high enough to recover no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, or higher if the POH says [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Do not teach stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. If you cannot get both the altitude and cloud clearance, change the lesson or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: The haze limits visibility. What do you change about clearing?
questions.a: Haze aggravates collision hazards in practice areas [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Clear at and below your altitude before each stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], raise the wing and look, and have the learner call 'clear' aloud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Share the lookout job [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: In the chop the stall horn chirps during the setup. How do you explain it to the learner?
questions.a: A gust can raise the AOA suddenly [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. It is a real warning: ease the back pressure and keep the descent stable. Use it to teach that the horn only gives a few knots of margin in typical airplanes [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

questions.q: At the first full stall the learner freezes with the yoke back and the left wing drops. What do you do?
questions.a: Take the controls, calmly saying 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], then reduce the AOA until the warning stops, roll the wings level with rudder against yaw, and add power as needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Practicing full stalls can lead to an inadvertent spin, which is why you guard the controls [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: Later, you want to add realism. What does AC 61-67C suggest for power-off stalls?
questions.a: Have the learner repeat the power-off stall while you distract them during the stall and recovery, then discuss the effect [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]]. Most stall/spin accidents come from distraction in routine flight [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

skills.do: Clear the area at and below your altitude before the maneuver, explaining why a stall needs a look below.
skills.practice: Fly your clearing turns with full callouts every time, as if a learner were copying you [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed "no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL)" and explain how you chose it.
skills.practice: On the ground, write down the practice area's highest terrain and your airplane's measured stall altitude loss, and work out the entry altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Configure in the approach or landing configuration the evaluator asks for and stay coordinated throughout, saying what you set and why.
skills.practice: Fly the maneuver at each flap setting, not just full flaps [[24:122|AFH 5-17]], calling out the ball position.

skills.do: Establish a stabilized descent at approach speed before raising the nose, while explaining why extra speed is a problem.
skills.practice: Hold altitude while slowing, then set the approach attitude, flaps and idle and trim [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]; talk through each step out loud.

skills.do: Transition smoothly from the approach or landing attitude to a stall-inducing pitch attitude, explaining the risk of pulling too fast.
skills.practice: Have another CFI watch for any yank on the entry, the accelerated stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: "Maintain a specified heading, ±10° if in straight flight; maintain a specified angle of bank not to exceed 20°, ±5° if in turning flight, until an impending or full stall occurs", while you keep talking.
skills.practice: Practice turning stalls at 15 to 20 degrees of bank while explaining; check the attitude indicator so talking does not let the bank wander [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall, such as buffet or the stall horn, out loud.
skills.practice: Name each cue as it appears on every practice stall: sight, sound, feel [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

skills.do: Recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall has occurred, as specified by the evaluator, explaining the order of the recovery.
skills.practice: Mix impending and full stalls every flight, repeating the request back before each [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY.
skills.practice: Rehearse the flap and gear retraction steps and speeds in the parked airplane, then fly them, flaps up in steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the evaluator specified.
skills.practice: Write the return targets on your kneeboard before each stall and fly back to them [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors when the evaluator, acting as a learner, makes them: name the error, say what you saw, and give the fix.
skills.practice: Fly with another instructor who makes AFH-listed errors on purpose; practice spotting each and giving a one-line fix [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Which statement about the critical angle of attack is correct?
options: It gets smaller as weight increases
A given airplane stalls at the same AOA regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude
It is higher in a turn
It is lower with an aft CG
quiz.why: A given aircraft always stalls at the same AOA regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

quiz.q: The PHAK lists conditions for which the published 1 G stall speed holds. Which is NOT one of them?
options: A standard day at sea level
quiz.why: The conditions are unaccelerated 1 G flight, coordinated flight and one weight [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]]; the AFH adds one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

quiz.q: Using the PHAK stall speed table, gear and flaps down and wings level, how much lower is the stall speed with power ON than with power OFF?
quiz.why: Gear and flaps down, level: power on 47 knots, power off 57 knots, so 57 - 47 = 10 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

quiz.q: Which wing planform gives little advance warning of a complete stall?
quiz.why: The elliptical wing gives little advance warning of a complete stall, and lateral control may be difficult [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

quiz.q: Which item does the AFH list as a limit on AOA indicator effectiveness?
quiz.why: Calibration, unheated probes or vanes, indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination can limit an AOA indicator [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

quiz.q: In a microburst on approach, why is reducing power and lowering the nose for the headwind shear dangerous?
options: It leaves the airplane nose-low and power-low when the tailwind shear arrives
quiz.why: The pilot is left nose-low and power-low when the tailwind shear occurs, which can cause a stall or a landing short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

quiz.q: In the AFH template, what comes right after disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot?
options: Pitch nose-down until the impending stall indications are eliminated
quiz.why: Push forward to reduce the AOA until the impending stall indications are gone before going on [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. In a trainer without an autopilot this is the actual first step.

quiz.q: What are the four phases of the demonstration-performance method in the AIH's flight instruction chapter?
options: Explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, evaluation
quiz.why: The method is divided into explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

quiz.q: What do the NTSB statistics in the AIH say about intentional stall and spin practice?
options: It seldom resulted in an accident; the real danger was inadvertent stalls from distractions
It should be banned below 5,000 ft
It is only dangerous in low-wing airplanes
quiz.why: The intentional practice of stalls and spins seldom resulted in an accident; inadvertent stalls induced by distraction were the real danger [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: What is the safest action when a learner overshoots the turn from base to final?
options: Add inside rudder to bring the nose around
Raise the nose to slow down
quiz.why: The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; avoid banks over 30 degrees this low and do not skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: On the CFI checkride the evaluator asks for a power-off stall but does not say impending or full. What should already have happened?
options: Nothing; you always fly a full stall
You and the evaluator should have reviewed this Area of Operation in the preflight briefing
You choose the impending stall because it is safer
final_quiz.why: The evaluator has discretion to ask for recovery at the first indication or after a full stall, and the applicant and evaluator must review this area in the preflight briefing (CFI ACS Appendix 3). Training should use the same recovery technique for both [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's power-off stall loses 350 ft in the recovery and holds no altitude. Under the CFI ACS, is that alone unsatisfactory?
options: Yes, more than 100 ft is unsatisfactory
No, the evaluation should not mandate a set altitude loss or holding altitude
Only if it is a full stall
final_quiz.why: Evaluation criteria should not mandate a predetermined altitude loss or maintaining altitude (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task C note). Some altitude loss is expected [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

final_quiz.q: During the learner tells, learner does step, your learner makes a small error that is not yet dangerous. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Safety permitting, let them go part way into the mistake and find the way out
final_quiz.why: Correcting errors does not mean taking over immediately; it is often better to let learners progress part way into the mistake and find a way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: A learner flies perfect power-off stalls but you suspect rote learning. What check does the AIH suggest?
options: Have them vary the maneuver slightly or combine it with another
Repeat the same stall ten more times
final_quiz.why: Require the learner to vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations or apply its elements elsewhere; without understanding they probably cannot [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: During a full stall demo your learner, frightened, grabs the yoke and pulls. What is the right response?
options: Calmly say 'I have the flight controls' and take them
Talk them through the recovery while both hold the yoke
final_quiz.why: Take the controls and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be very strong, and there is nothing to gain from fighting for the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's turning power-off stall is slipping at the break. What should you expect?
options: The outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly
final_quiz.why: If the airplane slips, the outer wing may stall first and move downward abruptly; in a skid the bank may increase [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: After recovering a full-flap power-off stall, your learner holds a higher-than-normal climb pitch with the flaps still down. What does AC 61-67C say may happen?
final_quiz.why: Attempting to climb with flaps extended at a higher than normal climb pitch can produce a secondary stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about a stall warning horn is best supported by the sources?
options: It always sounds exactly 5 knots before the stall
Many devices warn 4 to 8 knots early, but some airplanes rely on buffet and ice can remove the cues
It works the same with ice on the wing
final_quiz.why: Many devices alert 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]; many airplanes use buffet instead of a device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]; ice can bring a stall with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]].

final_quiz.q: Departing a high, hot airport, the climb stops and the horn sounds as the pilot keeps raising the nose. What is happening?
options: The airplane is running out of energy; power available is less than power required
final_quiz.why: In the AFH scenario the airplane slows past the point where it stops climbing and the horn sounds where power available is less than power required [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

final_quiz.q: In a single-engine trainer with no autopilot or spoilers, which template steps apply?
options: Reduce AOA, roll wings level, add power as needed, return to the flightpath
Add power, reduce AOA, level the wings
Disconnect autopilot, reduce AOA, retract spoilers
final_quiz.why: Such an airplane uses four of the six steps: reduce AOA until the warning stops, roll level, add power while coordinated, return to the flightpath [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

final_quiz.q: You plan stalls on a marginal VFR day. What does the AIH say you should do as the instructor?
options: Fly the lesson but stay lower
Coach the learner to identify the risks, such as entering IMC or practicing too low, and discuss options like a pattern lesson, simulator, ground school or rescheduling
Practice stalls in the traffic pattern
final_quiz.why: The instructor should coach the learner to identify those risks and discuss mitigations such as changing the lesson, using a simulation device or ground school, or rescheduling [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: Why does AC 61-67C single out distractions as part of stall training?
options: They are required on every checkride maneuver
Simulating scenarios with distractions is the most effective training method from the FAA stall awareness study
They replace the need for clearing turns
final_quiz.why: The most effective training method in the FAA stall awareness study is simulating scenarios that lead to inadvertent stalls by creating distractions [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]].

final_quiz.q: Before giving instruction in an airplane with an AOA indicator, what does the AFH ask of instructors?
options: Get training from an instructor knowledgeable about AOA indicators
final_quiz.why: Ground and flight instructors should make every attempt to get training from an instructor knowledgeable about AOA indicators first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

takeaways: A wing stalls when it passes its critical AOA, at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.
The power-off stall rehearses approach accidents: stretched glides, low or slow finals and base to final turns.
Recover in order: reduce AOA until the warning stops, wings level with rudder, power as needed, then the flightpath.
Stall warnings have limits: many airplanes have only buffet, and ice can remove the cues.
Teach with telling-and-doing, from impending to full and from straight to turning.
Brief the positive exchange of flight controls, guard the controls, and stay high enough and clear of clouds.
Add realistic distractions once the basic stall is solid; that is where real stalls come from.
cfi_notes: AC 61-67C paragraph 105 (2000) describes reducing AOA, then applying maximum allowable power, then establishing straight and level flight [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. The newer AFH template rolls the wings level before power and adds power 'as needed' [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Both put AOA first. Teach the AFH template as adapted by your POH, and show the difference if a learner reads the AC.
AC 61-67C says a 60-degree level turn raises stall speed by 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]]; the square root of 2 is about 1.414, so 41 percent, as the AFH states, is closer [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
The PHAK lists three conditions for the published 1 G stall speed [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]]; the AFH lists four, adding one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Teach the AFH's four.

The 4 to 8 knot stall warning margin is a typical figure from AC 61-67C [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. The current rule requires only a clear warning with sufficient margin and gives no number [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]]. Measure your own airplane's margin with your learner.

In a power-off stall many trainers break gently, and the main cue may be the yoke on the stop and a high sink rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Learners waiting for a sharp break may hold the stall too long; tell them what the break looks like in your airplane.
Many learners mix up 'recover at the horn' and 'hold to the break'. Have them repeat the request back before every stall, and give both kinds on each flight.

The AIH distraction list and the AC 61-67C list are almost the same [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(10)]]. Use them during the setup and the recovery, never in a way that removes the guard on the controls.

The AIH reminds you that a pilot in command must know when to tell anyone, even a DPE, that their actions are distracting and interfering with safe flight [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Model that on your checkride.
gaps: None of these sources defines which flap setting counts as the 'approach configuration' the ACS mentions. Use the POH and agree it with the evaluator.
No source gives a typical altitude loss for a power-off stall in a light single. Measure your airplane's and use it to plan entry altitudes.
The sources do not give exact words to brief before a stall or a standard way to handle a learner who freezes, beyond the positive exchange of controls. Write your own and use it every time.
The stall speeds, warning margin, wing-drop tendency and recovery for your airplane come from the POH/AFM; the PHAK table and AFH template are generic.
The sources do not say how many repetitions a learner needs before full stalls or turning stalls; that is your judgment and the syllabus.

activities.title: Stall speed numbers you will use in the brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: PHAK table: gear and flaps down, power off, wings level stall speed is 57 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, and in a level turn the load factor is 1 divided by the cosine of the bank angle. Predict the stall speed at 20 degrees of bank, the steepest the ACS allows for this Task.
Same method at 30 degrees of bank, starting from 57 knots. What do you predict? (The table prints 62.)
items.why: 1 / cos 30 = 1.155. Square root = 1.075. 57 x 1.075 = 61.3, about 61 knots, within a knot of the printed 62 [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

items.q: The PHAK says stalling speed rises by about one half at about 63 degrees of bank. Check it: by what percent does stall speed rise at 63 degrees in a level turn?
items.why: 1 / cos 63 = 2.203. Square root = 1.484, a 48 percent increase, about one half [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

items.q: A learner's airplane stalls at 50 knots at 1 G. In a sloppy recovery they pull 2 G. Below about what speed will that pull stall the wing again?
items.why: 50 x square root of 2 = 50 x 1.414 = 70.7, about 71 knots [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. That is a secondary stall in the making [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

items.q: The highest terrain in your practice area is 1,240 ft MSL. Your airplane loses about 350 ft in a power-off stall recovery. What is the lowest entry altitude that keeps the recovery at or above 1,500 ft AGL?
items.why: 1,240 + 1,500 + 350 = 3,090 ft MSL (AI.X.C.S2) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The 350 ft loss is a given for this problem, not a source number.

activities.title: Read the AOA indicator
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.title: True or false: stall warnings
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Certification rules allow the stall warning to be aerodynamic buffet instead of a device.
cards.why: True. Manufacturers may provide it through inherent aerodynamic qualities (pre-stall buffet) or a device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: In icing, the stall usually comes earlier on the horn and at a lower airspeed.
cards.why: False. It may come with little or none of the usual cues, at a lower AOA and well above normal stall airspeed [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102b]].

cards.s: All AOA indicators take flap position into account.
cards.why: False. Some do, but not all [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: An autopilot can hide some stall cues from the pilot.
cards.why: True. Its control inputs may mask tactile cues or try to control the airplane in the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102c]].

cards.s: At the proper landing attitude in the flare, the airplane is approaching a stall.
cards.why: True. At the landing attitude the airplane is approaching a stall as the critical AOA nears [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

cards.s: Vision is the most reliable cue to an impending stall.
cards.why: False. The airplane can be stalled in any attitude, so vision is not foolproof [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

activities.title: CFI checkride: the evaluator plays your learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI applicant in the right seat. The evaluator flies as a private pilot learner on a first power-off stall lesson, and will make mistakes for you to catch. The practice area terrain tops out at 1,600 ft MSL.

steps.s: Before taking off, what must the ground brief include besides the procedure?
options: The positive exchange of flight controls and the safety procedures
A promise that stalls are not frightening
steps.why: The preflight briefing should include procedures for the exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], and the explanation phase should cover safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

steps.s: Level at 2,900 ft MSL, the 'learner' starts slowing for the stall. What do you say?
options: Stop: climb so the recovery ends no lower than 3,100 ft MSL, then clear the area
Descend to see the ground better
Do the stall straight ahead only
steps.why: 1,600 + 1,500 = 3,100 ft MSL, so 2,900 is too low before any altitude loss [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] (AI.X.C.S2). Clear before the maneuver [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: At the break the 'learner' adds full power and right aileron first, with the nose still high. What do you say?
options: Nose down first until the horn stops, then wings level, then power
Pull back to stop the descent
steps.why: Recovering with power or leveling the wings before reducing AOA are listed errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; AOA first, then roll, then power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: On the next stall the 'learner' freezes, pulling back, and the left wing drops. What do you do?
options: Take the controls, saying 'I have the flight controls', and recover
Ask the learner to let go slowly
steps.why: Take control calmly with 'I have the flight controls'; there is nothing to gain fighting an anxious learner [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Then reduce AOA, level the wings and add power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: Back on the ground, how do you start the debrief?
options: Ask the learner to assess their own performance, then give yours and compare
Skip it; the flight went fine
steps.why: Collaborative assessment begins with a learner self-assessment, followed by the instructor's assessment and a comparison [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Give concrete fixes and avoid ending negative [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
